readerTitle: How a camera, not code, got Airbnb moving
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Airbnb 초기, 2007~2009) + 가상 적용 (사내 전문가 매칭 프로그램)
insight: 초기 마켓플레이스의 병목은 공급의 '양'보다 구매자가 믿고 고를 수 있는 공급의 '질'일 때가 많다. 가진 공급을 한 곳에서 손으로 고치는 것이 트래픽을 늘리는 것보다 먼저다.
misconception: 마켓플레이스가 안 크면 광고로 구매자를 더 데려오거나 판매자 수를 늘리면 된다. 확장할 수 없는 수작업은 시간 낭비다.

sources.text: Paul Graham, "Do Things That Don't Scale" (2013). 창업자들이 뉴욕에서 호스트를 직접 찾아가 사진을 찍은 일화
Airbnb Newsroom, company history (2007년 샌프란시스코 디자인 컨퍼런스 기간 에어매트리스 임대, 공동창업자)
Joe Gebbia 강연·인터뷰 (예: Y Combinator / Startup School 등). 뉴욕 사진 촬영 이후 매출이 약 두 배가 되었다는 본인 발언
Airbnb 전문 사진 촬영 프로그램 관련 언론 보도 (2010년 전후)

factChecks.note: 2007년 10월 샌프란시스코 디자인 컨퍼런스(IDSA) 기간 호텔이 가득 차 에어매트리스를 빌려준 일, 첫 손님 3명은 Airbnb 공식 역사 자료로 게시 전 재확인하세요.
뉴욕 방문 시점을 2009년 초 Y Combinator 기간으로 적었습니다. Paul Graham 에세이와 대조해 확인하세요.
'매출이 약 두 배가 되었다'는 Joe Gebbia 본인의 회고 발언입니다. 카드에는 'has said in later talks'로 표시했고 구체 금액은 넣지 않았습니다. 원 발언 출처를 확보하세요.
전문 사진가 프로그램의 정확한 시작 연도와 규모는 쓰지 않고 'later'로만 표현했습니다. 필요하면 보도자료로 확인 후 보완하세요.
'뉴욕 사진 상당수가 어둡고 작고 흐렸다'는 창업자들의 회고에 근거한 정성적 묘사입니다. 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Airbnb's first big fix wasn't code. It was a camera.
body: In October 2007, two designers in San Francisco were short on rent. A design conference had filled the city's hotels, so they put air mattresses on their floor and offered them with breakfast. Three guests came.
That was the start of Airbnb. The harder part came next: getting strangers to book strangers' homes, again and again.

image.label: Air mattresses on an apartment floor with a breakfast tray
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 아파트 거실 바닥에 에어매트리스 세 개, 그 옆에 아침 식사 쟁반. 창밖으로 도시 야경. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Growth is flat. What do you fix first?
body: By early 2009, the three founders had a working site and a place in Y Combinator, a startup program. But bookings were barely growing and money was tight.
Looking at New York, their most important city, they noticed many listing photos were dark, small or blurry, often taken on phones. What would you do?

options.text: Spend what money is left on ads to bring in more travelers
options.feedback: More visitors would arrive, but they'd meet the same unclear listings. You'd pay for traffic that leaves without booking.

options.text: Fly to New York, meet hosts and photograph their homes yourselves
options.feedback: It costs time that doesn't scale, but it fixes what guests actually see and teaches you what hosts struggle with. This is what they did.

options.text: Email every host a guide on taking better photos
options.feedback: Cheap and scalable, but most busy hosts won't act on an email. You'd also learn nothing about why they posted weak photos.

cards.title: They went to New York themselves.
body: The founders flew to New York, met hosts in person and photographed their homes with a rented camera. They also stayed with hosts and asked what made hosting hard.
Joe Gebbia has said in later talks that revenue there roughly doubled soon after. Airbnb later turned the idea into a program that sent professional photographers to hosts' homes.

image.label: A founder with a camera photographing a bright guest room
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 어둡고 흐린 휴대폰 사진 속 방, 오른쪽에는 밝게 정리된 같은 방의 사진. 가운데에 카메라를 든 사람. 실제 인물 얼굴이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A listing nobody trusts isn't really supply.
body: In a marketplace, **liquidity** means a buyer who shows up has a good chance of finding something and completing a deal. It's tempting to measure it by count: how many listings, how many sellers.

Airbnb's New York problem wasn't count. Travelers could see listings but couldn't judge them. A blurry photo of a stranger's spare room asks a guest to take a big risk on little information. Better photos turned listings that existed on paper into listings people would book.

cards.title: One trip did three jobs.
body: Taking the photos by hand helped in ways an ad budget couldn't.
list: **Trust:** guests could finally see what they would get
**Learning:** hosts described problems no website data would show
**Focus:** one city, so every improved listing made local searches better
cards.callout: Paul Graham later used this trip as a main example in his essay "Do Things That Don't Scale."

cards.title: Hand work is a test, not the business.
body: Going door to door worked because the founders had found the real bottleneck. If a market's real problem is too few buyers, hand-polishing listings just gives you prettier pages nobody visits.

It also can't last. Three founders can't photograph every home in the world. Airbnb kept the idea by paying photographers, a cost it could carry once bookings grew. Start by hand, then decide what is worth turning into a system.

cards.title: Now it's an internal help marketplace.
body: You run a program at a 3,000-person company. Employees can book an hour with an in-house expert on data, contracts or pricing. About 80 experts signed up, but requests are rare. Most profiles show only a name and a job title.
You have one month. What do you do?

options.text: Send a company-wide email promoting the program
options.feedback: Visits may jump, but people will meet the same thin profiles and leave unsure who can help. You spend attention you can't easily win back.

options.text: Pick one department, sit with its 15 experts and rewrite their profiles together, with real examples of problems they've solved
options.feedback: Slow and narrow, but it gives colleagues a reason to trust a booking and shows you what experts need. Then you can repeat it elsewhere.

options.text: Build a rating system so the best experts rise to the top
options.feedback: Ratings build trust over time, but they need bookings first. With few requests, most experts would have nothing to show.

cards.title: Make the supply you have worth choosing.
body: Early on, a marketplace often grows faster by fixing what buyers see than by adding more buyers or sellers.
**Try it today:** look at your offer through a new customer's eyes. Find one thing a stranger can't judge from what you show them, and fix it by hand for your top five listings, products or people.
